title: Multiple Linear Regression I: Comparative Chapter Matrix

fields.name: central_concept
fields.description: Primary analytical topic and model framework.
fields.example: Multiple linear regression models a response using several explanatory variables and is linear in parameters.

fields.name: model_form
fields.description: Core regression-function and fitted-model form presented.

fields.name: estimation_method
fields.example: Least squares minimizes \(SS(\mathbf b^{*})=(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\mathbf b^{*})'(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\mathbf b^{*})\); if \(\mathbf X'\mathbf X\) is invertible, \(\mathbf b=(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X'\mathbf y\).

fields.name: data_representation
fields.description: Notation used to organize observations, responses, and explanatory variables.
fields.example: Each observation is \((x_{i1},\ldots,x_{ik},y_i)\); \(\mathbf y\) is \(n\times1\) and \(\mathbf X\) is \(n\times(k+1)\), typically with intercept column \(x_{i0}=1\).

fields.name: model_assumptions
fields.description: Sampling and error assumptions underlying the multiple linear regression model.
fields.example: Fixed explanatory variables; \(\textrm{E}y_i=\beta_0+\cdots+\beta_kx_{ik}\); constant variance \(\sigma^2\); independent responses or errors; normal responses or errors.

fields.name: estimator_properties
fields.description: Theoretical properties established for least-squares coefficient estimators.
fields.example: Under F1--F4, \(\mathbf b\) is unbiased and \(\operatorname{Var}\mathbf b=\sigma^2(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}\); Gauss-Markov gives minimum variance among linear unbiased estimators; under F1--F5, \(\mathbf b\) is normal.

fields.name: goodness_of_fit
fields.description: Fit statistics, sums-of-squares decomposition, and their interpretations.

fields.name: inference_method
fields.example: Test \(H_0:\beta_j=0\) using \(t(b_j)=b_j/se(b_j)\) with \(df=n-(k+1)\); a confidence interval is \(b_j\pm t_{n-(k+1),1-\alpha/2}se(b_j)\).

fields.name: multivariate_diagnostic
fields.description: Graphical and numerical tools for assessing conditional relationships among variables.
fields.example: An added variable plot graphs residuals from \(y\) on other variables against residuals from \(x_j\) on other variables; its correlation is the partial correlation coefficient.

fields.name: partial_correlation_relation
fields.description: Relationship between partial correlation and a regression coefficient t-ratio.

fields.name: special_explanatory_variables
fields.description: Types of explanatory-variable constructions supported by the linear-in-parameters framework.
fields.example: Binary or indicator variables; polynomial and logarithmic transformations; interactions; piecewise linear or broken-stick terms with kinks.

fields.name: key_empirical_examples
fields.description: Applied datasets and substantive contexts used to illustrate the methods.
fields.example: Term life insurance demand; female life-expectancy advantage across countries; refrigerator prices; life insurance company expenses; charitable contributions and wages; stockbroker commissions.

fields.name: exercise_topics
fields.description: Numbered exercise applications and requested analytical tasks.
fields.example: 3.1--3.3 compute ANOVA, fit, standard-error, covariance, and t-statistic quantities; 3.4 Wisconsin Lottery; 3.5 Insurance Company Expenses; 3.6 National Life Expectancies.

data.central_concept: Multiple linear regression extends linear regression to several explanatory variables, fitting a regression plane and permitting nonlinear functions of explanatory variables while retaining linearity in parameters.
data.estimation_method: Method of least squares minimizes \(SS(b_0^*,\ldots,b_k^*)=\sum_{i=1}^n[y_i-(b_0^*+b_1^*x_{i1}+\cdots+b_k^*x_{ik})]^2\); normal equations are \(\mathbf X'\mathbf X\mathbf b=\mathbf X'\mathbf y\); unique solution \(\mathbf b=(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X'\mathbf y\) when explanatory variables are not linear combinations of one another.
data.data_representation: Data consist of \(k\) explanatory variables and one response for each of \(n\) observations: \((x_{i1},\ldots,x_{ik},y_i)\); \(\mathbf y\) is the \(n\times1\) response vector and \(\mathbf X\) is the \(n\times(k+1)\) explanatory-variable matrix.
data.model_assumptions: Observables representation F1--F5: linear conditional mean; nonstochastic \(x\)'s; \(\operatorname{Var}y_i=\sigma^2\); independent \(y_i\)'s; normally distributed \(y_i\)'s. Error representation E1--E5: additive errors; nonstochastic \(x\)'s; \(\textrm{E}\varepsilon_i=0\), \(\operatorname{Var}\varepsilon_i=\sigma^2\); independent and normal errors.
data.estimator_properties: Property 1: under F1--F4, \(\mathbf b\) is unbiased for \(\boldsymbol\beta\). Property 2: \(\operatorname{Var}\mathbf b=\sigma^2(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}\). Gauss-Markov: least squares is minimum variance unbiased among estimators linear in responses. Property 3: under F1--F5, \(\mathbf b\) is normally distributed.
data.goodness_of_fit: Residuals are \(e_i=y_i-\widehat y_i\); \(s^2=\sum_{i=1}^ne_i^2/[n-(k+1)]\) is MSE and \(s\) is residual standard deviation. \(\text{Total SS}=\text{Error SS}+\text{Regression SS}\); \(R^2=\text{Regression SS}/\text{Total SS}\); \(R_a^2=1-[(\text{Error SS})/[n-(k+1)]]/[(\text{Total SS})/(n-1)]\).
data.inference_method: For \(H_0:\beta_j=d\), use \(t\text{-ratio}=(b_j-d)/se(b_j)\), where \(se(b_j)=s\sqrt{\text{the }(j+1)\text{st diagonal element of }(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}}\). For a two-sided test reject when \(|t\text{-ratio}|>t_{n-(k+1),1-\alpha/2}\); confidence interval \(b_j\pm t_{n-(k+1),1-\alpha/2}se(b_j)\).
data.multivariate_diagnostic: Scatterplot and correlation matrices summarize only pairs of variables. Added variable plots control for other explanatory variables: regress \(y\) on all variables except \(x_j\), regress \(x_j\) on those same variables, then plot the first residuals against the second. Omitted variables can yield misleading coefficient significance or signs.
data.partial_correlation_relation: The partial correlation is the correlation between the two residual series in an added variable plot and measures the relationship between \(y\) and \(x_j\) in the presence of other explanatory variables. It can be calculated as \(t(b_j)/\sqrt{t(b_j)^2+n-(k+1)}\).
data.special_explanatory_variables: Binary variables are indicators or dummy variables, with coefficients interpreted as changes from the base category. Transformations include powers \(x,x^2,\ldots,x^p\), \(\ln x\), and categorized continuous variables. Interaction terms such as \(x_1x_2\) allow marginal effects to depend on other variables. Piecewise linear models use binary variables and interactions to represent kinks or discontinuities.
data.key_empirical_examples: Term Life Insurance: \(n=275\), LNFACE modeled using EDUCATION, NUMHH, and LNINCOME; fitted plane \(\widehat y=2.584+0.206x_1+0.306x_2+0.494x_3\). Female advantage: Lemaire's model of life-expectancy differences across 169 countries. Refrigerator Prices: \(n=37\), illustrating ECOST's positive marginal correlation but negative controlled coefficient. Life Insurance Company Expenses: Segal's output, quadratic, binary-interaction, and input-price model.
data.exercise_topics: Exercise 3.1: fictitious ANOVA and \(R^2\) calculations. Exercise 3.2: standard error, covariance, correlation, and variance calculations from \((\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}\). Exercise 3.3: small two-variable regression. Exercise 3.4: Wisconsin Lottery regression and added-variable analysis. Exercise 3.5: NAIC insurance-company expense models. Exercise 3.6: national life expectancies using FERTILITY, PUBLICEDUCATION, and lnHEALTH.
